newsitem.title: USA: Dollar posts gains vs mark and yen at U.S. open.
newsitem.headline: Dollar posts gains vs mark and yen at U.S. open.

text.p: The dollar opened higher against the mark and yen, bolstered by predictions of a stronger greenback by German economic pundits and options-related activity, currency experts said.
On Tuesday, Germany's six leading economic research institutes said in their semiannual report they see the dollar averaging 1.80 marks in 1998.
"Certainly it was more dollar positive, but I still think we could see lower levels (in the dollar-mark exchange rate)," said Paul Park, a vice president of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank N.A.

Park said dollar-mark is "really at the mercy of a lot of the political events" such as the upcoming French elections and uncertainty about the prospects for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). In this environment, he said the dollar could pull back to 1.6850 marks.
Early parliamentary elections in France will be held on May 25 and June 1, 10 months ahead of scheduled.
The dollar opened at 1.7065/75 marks and 126.15/25 yen, up from 1.6980/85 marks and 125.32/37 yen at Monday's close.
Some experts linked dollar/mark gains to anticipation of World Bank/International Monetary Fund meetings this weekend.
Finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial powers will also meet on the fringes of the IMF gathering in Washington.

"The market is anticipating a bit of a talk up of the EMU timetable by European officials at this weekend's IMF meeting...," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International. "The market may be backtracking a bit on yesterday's doubts about the EMU project," McCarthy added.
Indeed Bundesbank Vice President Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum said on Tuesday it would be no problem to launch EMU with a smaller number of countries if that provided stability.
A trader at the New York branch of a major Japanese bank attributed gains in the dollar versus the yen, in part, to increases in the greenback against the German currency.
"Basically, dollar/yen is pulled (higher) by dollar/mark," the trader said.
In addition, the trader noted that a Japanese institution sold a large option to sell dollars at 124.50 yen and 127.50 yen. The option expires on April 25 in Tokyo, the trader said.
"So, they have to buy above 125 (yen) to defend the option," the trader said. "That's why 125 (yen has been) very biddish."
Looking ahead, some traders expected the dollar to remain mired in current ranges.

"I think that we're going to see continued consolidation here," Park said. Perhaps the dollar will take its cue from U.S stocks and bonds, he said. "If U.S. asset markets get hit pretty hard, we could see some weakness" in the dollar.

Elsewhere, the dollar opened at 1.4518/28 Swiss francs, up from 1.4413/23 francs. Sterling rose to $1.6358/68 from $1.6350/60. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3960/65 from C$1.3984/89. The Australian dollar climbed to $0.7785/90 from $0.7772/77. ((-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668))
